passages.title: What is Digestion
passages.text: Digestion is the process of breaking down complex, insoluble food molecules into simple, soluble substances that can be absorbed into the blood. It involves mechanical digestion, such as chewing and churning, and chemical digestion by enzymes. The human digestive system consists of the alimentary canal and associated glands such as the salivary glands, liver and pancreas.

passages.title: Digestion in the Mouth
passages.text: Digestion begins in the mouth where teeth mechanically break food into smaller pieces and the tongue mixes it with saliva. Saliva contains the enzyme salivary amylase (ptyalin) which begins the breakdown of starch into maltose. Saliva also lubricates the food to form a bolus that can be swallowed easily.

passages.title: Types of Teeth
passages.text: Humans have four types of teeth: incisors for cutting, canines for tearing, premolars and molars for grinding and crushing food. This mechanical breakdown increases the surface area of food so that enzymes can act more efficiently during chemical digestion.

passages.title: Oesophagus and Peristalsis
passages.text: The oesophagus is a muscular tube that carries the bolus from the mouth to the stomach. Food is pushed along by peristalsis, which is a series of rhythmic wave-like muscular contractions and relaxations of the gut wall. Peristalsis moves food through the entire alimentary canal.

passages.title: Digestion in the Stomach
passages.text: The stomach is a muscular J-shaped organ that stores and churns food. It secretes gastric juice containing hydrochloric acid, the enzyme pepsin and mucus. Hydrochloric acid kills bacteria and provides the acidic pH needed for pepsin to digest proteins into smaller peptides. Mucus protects the stomach lining from the acid.

passages.title: Role of HCl and Pepsin
passages.text: Hydrochloric acid in the stomach creates a strongly acidic environment (about pH 2) that activates pepsinogen into the active enzyme pepsin and kills most microorganisms in food. Pepsin is a protease enzyme that breaks down proteins into shorter chains of amino acids called peptides.

passages.title: The Small Intestine
passages.text: The small intestine is the main site of digestion and absorption. It is divided into the duodenum, jejunum and ileum. In the duodenum, bile from the liver and enzymes from the pancreas complete the digestion of carbohydrates, proteins and fats. The jejunum and ileum are where most absorption of nutrients occurs.

passages.title: Role of the Pancreas
passages.text: The pancreas secretes pancreatic juice into the duodenum. It contains pancreatic amylase to digest starch, trypsin to digest proteins, and lipase to digest fats. Pancreatic juice is alkaline and helps neutralise the acidic chyme arriving from the stomach so that enzymes can work in the correct pH.

passages.title: Liver, Bile and Gallbladder
passages.text: The liver produces bile, which is stored and concentrated in the gallbladder before being released into the duodenum. Bile does not contain enzymes but emulsifies large fat droplets into smaller ones, increasing their surface area so that lipase can digest them more efficiently. Bile also neutralises stomach acid.

passages.title: Villi and Absorption
passages.text: The inner wall of the small intestine is folded into tiny finger-like projections called villi, each covered with microvilli. Villi greatly increase the surface area for absorption. Each villus contains blood capillaries that absorb glucose and amino acids and a lacteal that absorbs fatty acids and glycerol.

passages.title: The Large Intestine
passages.text: The large intestine, or colon, absorbs water and mineral salts from the undigested food, turning it into semi-solid faeces. It also houses beneficial bacteria that produce some vitamins. The faeces are stored in the rectum and expelled through the anus during egestion.

passages.title: Absorption of Nutrients
passages.text: Absorption is the passage of digested food molecules through the wall of the small intestine into the blood and lymph. Glucose and amino acids pass into blood capillaries in the villi, while fatty acids and glycerol enter the lacteals. The absorbed nutrients are then transported to body cells.

passages.title: Assimilation
passages.text: Assimilation is the process by which absorbed nutrients are used by body cells for energy, growth and repair. For example, glucose is used in respiration to release energy, amino acids are used to build proteins, and fats are stored or used as an energy reserve.

passages.title: Digestive Enzymes
passages.text: Digestive enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up the breakdown of food. Carbohydrases such as amylase break down starch into sugars, proteases such as pepsin and trypsin break down proteins into amino acids, and lipases break down fats into fatty acids and glycerol.

passages.title: Peristalsis
passages.text: Peristalsis is the wave-like contraction and relaxation of the smooth muscles lining the alimentary canal. It pushes food forward from the oesophagus through the stomach and intestines. Peristalsis works even against gravity, which is why food can be swallowed while lying down.

qa.question: What is digestion?
qa.answer: Digestion is the breakdown of complex, insoluble food into simple, soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the blood.

qa.question: Where does digestion begin?
qa.answer: Digestion begins in the mouth, where teeth break food mechanically and salivary amylase begins digesting starch.

qa.question: What is the function of saliva?
qa.answer: Saliva lubricates food and contains salivary amylase (ptyalin) which begins the breakdown of starch into maltose.

qa.question: What are the four types of teeth and their functions?
qa.answer: Incisors cut, canines tear, and premolars and molars grind and crush food.

qa.question: What is the role of hydrochloric acid in the stomach?
qa.answer: Hydrochloric acid kills bacteria and provides the acidic pH needed to activate and allow pepsin to digest proteins.

qa.question: What does pepsin do?
qa.answer: Pepsin is a protease enzyme in the stomach that breaks down proteins into smaller peptides.

qa.question: What are the three parts of the small intestine?
qa.answer: The small intestine is divided into the duodenum, jejunum and ileum.

qa.question: What is the role of bile in digestion?
qa.answer: Bile emulsifies large fat droplets into smaller ones, increasing surface area for lipase, and neutralises stomach acid. It contains no enzymes.

qa.question: What enzymes does the pancreas produce?
qa.answer: The pancreas produces pancreatic amylase (starch), trypsin (proteins) and lipase (fats).

qa.question: What are villi and what is their function?
qa.answer: Villi are finger-like projections in the small intestine that increase surface area for the absorption of digested nutrients into blood capillaries and lacteals.

qa.question: What is the function of the large intestine?
qa.answer: The large intestine absorbs water and mineral salts from undigested food and forms semi-solid faeces.

qa.question: What is peristalsis?
qa.answer: Peristalsis is the wave-like muscular contraction and relaxation that pushes food along the alimentary canal.

qa.question: What is the difference between absorption and assimilation?
qa.answer: Absorption is the passage of digested nutrients into the blood, while assimilation is the use of those nutrients by body cells for energy, growth and repair.

qa.question: Which enzyme digests fats and what are the products?
qa.answer: Lipase digests fats into fatty acids and glycerol.

qa.question: Why is the small intestine well adapted for absorption?
qa.answer: It is long and lined with villi and microvilli which greatly increase surface area, and it has a rich blood supply and thin walls for efficient absorption.

qa.question: What is the function of the gallbladder?
qa.answer: The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile produced by the liver before releasing it into the duodenum.

qa.question: True or False: Bile contains digestive enzymes.
qa.answer: False. Bile contains no enzymes; it emulsifies fats to help lipase work.

qa.question: What is the role of the liver in digestion?
qa.answer: The liver produces bile which emulsifies fats, and it also processes absorbed nutrients such as storing glucose as glycogen.

qa.question: What is a bolus?
qa.answer: A bolus is the soft, rounded mass of chewed food mixed with saliva that is swallowed and moved into the oesophagus.
